## Today

- Why republics and democracies arose
- What they replaced
- How representative government works the idea
- Republic, democracy, and minority rights — including property

# Why This Matters

## Why This Matters

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 46px;"}
By the end of today you will explain why republics and democracies arose against abusive executives, define both terms, and show how representative government plus minority rights — including property — are two sides of the same project.
:::

# Why

## The problem was the executive

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 48px;"}
Kings turned tyrant — wealthy stationary bandits plundering those beneath them
:::

## Not a war on earned wealth

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 48px;"}
Property rights protection *for* earned wealth — against predation from above
:::

## Legitimate government and property

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 46px;"}
Government exists to secure life, liberty, and property — not to be the chief predator
:::

# What

## Overthrow and evolution

- Rome: overthrow of kings
- Britain / Europe: evolution of parliaments and councils

First upper classes constrain the king — later towns, then commoners gain representation and rights.

# How

## Elected representative government

::: {.custom-style style="font-size: 48px;"}
Congress and legislatures as the institutional answer to unconstrained executives
:::

# Definitions

## Democracy

Rule by the people.

## Republic

*Res publica* — the public thing; government as the people's common affair.

"Republic means not a monarchy" is largely a historical accident of labeling. Both were reactions to abusive executives.

# Aristotle and Madison

For Aristotle, "democracy" could mean rule by the many for themselves — a corrupt form.

Federalist 10: representation and a larger sphere filter faction; pure democracy amplifies it. Madison's "democracy" ≈ direct assembly. Today's "liberal democracy" is much closer to what he called a republic.

# Two sides of the same coin

Republic and democracy converge when minority rights — including property — are protected. Against the stationary bandit and against majority plunder alike.

# Suffrage and property

Britain: Parliament from 1215 (great barons) to 1928 (full women's suffrage). United States: 1789 already much broader than "barons only" → 1920 full women's suffrage.

Secure rights → invest → real wealth. Education is an investment. Protection of broad-based property rights and expansion of democracy support broad-based prosperity.

# Discussion

- Is the United States a democracy, a republic, or both — and what hinges on minority (including property) rights?
- Why did constraining the executive come before full popular suffrage in the European story?
- How is your education an "investment" in the property-rights story?
